comments.text:
Some of what Matt presents here is historically accurate — Dahomey's role in the slave trade, the Barbary slave trade, and the global history of slavery are all legitimate topics that deserve more attention. But the framing undermines the facts.

The video opens by explicitly saying its goal is to counter a "demoralization campaign." That's not history — that's a predetermined conclusion dressed up as history. When you start with the goal of making one group feel better, you're doing the same thing you're accusing others of doing, just in reverse.

A few specific issues:

- Calling American slavery a "best case scenario" because the enslaved population grew after 1808 is a deeply strange metric. Population growth was partly the result of enslaved women being systematically sexually exploited to produce more enslaved people. That's not a sign of good conditions.

- The "only 1.2% owned slaves" statistic is technically true but misleading. The entire Southern legal, economic, and political system was built to protect and expand slavery. You didn't need to own slaves to benefit from or enforce that system.

- Legitimate historians do study Dahomey, the Barbary trade, and white indentured servitude. The fact that these topics exist in academic literature contradicts the premise that they're being suppressed.

You can acknowledge that slavery was a global institution without using that fact to minimize what happened in America. Both things can be true.

comments.text: As an African, this history is not new to me, fortunately. What I appreciate about this video is that it broadens the historical lens. It helps us to acknowledge that human exploitation was not exclusive to one race, one region, or one era. Black, white, and other groups have endured brutal systems of oppression at different points in history. Recognizing this does not erase anyone’s suffering. It adds deeper context. It also challenges the oversimplified narratives that reduce history to a single story of permanent victim (blacks) and permanent oppressor (whites). When we understand that cruelty has crossed racial and geographic lines, we move closer to maturity in how we discuss the past, right? The real takeaway is this: suffering is part of human history, not owned or reserved for one group. comments.text:
A note to viewers who genuinely want the full picture:

I’ll give Walsh this. Some of what he presents is historically documented. African kingdoms like Dahomey did participate in the slave trade. Arab and Islamic slave trades were massive. Slavery existed in ancient Babylon, Greece, Rome, and across every continent. These are facts. And if your education left them out, that’s a real failure worth addressing.

But here’s where Walsh crosses the line from educator to propagandist, and it’s worth understanding exactly how he does it, because it’s sophisticated.

The Statistical Sleight of Hand

Walsh emphasizes that only about 4% of the 12.5 million enslaved Africans transported to the New World arrived in the United States, roughly 450,000 to 472,000 people. Technically accurate. But here’s what he doesn’t tell you: by 1860, that 450,000 had become 4 million enslaved people on American soil. Why? Because unlike Brazil and the Caribbean where enslaved people were worked to death and replaced, the American system was engineered for natural reproduction. Enslavers had a financial incentive to keep people alive long enough to breed more enslaved people. This isn’t “milder.” It’s a different architecture of dehumanization, one that turned human beings into a self-replicating asset class. The low import number is actually evidence of how deeply institutionalized American slavery became, not evidence of its comparative gentleness.

The Dahomey Deflection

Yes, Dahomey was brutal. Yes, they raided neighbors and sold captives. This is documented and real. But here is what Walsh systematically omits: Dahomey sold captives to European buyers who created the demand. The Transatlantic slave trade existed because European colonial economies needed mass unpaid labor to generate wealth at scale. Before European demand, African inter-tribal warfare produced captives who were typically integrated into local societies, not shipped across an ocean in chains with a 15 to 20% mortality rate just on the crossing (the Middle Passage). Walsh presents African agency in the slave trade without presenting the economic architecture that incentivized and scaled it. That’s not history. That’s selective prosecution.

Whites Ended Slavery: The Incomplete Verdict

Walsh’s closing argument is that European Christian nations deserve credit for abolishing slavery globally. Britain’s West Africa Squadron, the American Civil War, French troops ending Dahomey’s practices. This framing has two critical problems:

	1.	European powers created the modern Transatlantic slave trade in the first place. Crediting Europe for ending what Europe industrialized is like crediting an arsonist for calling the fire department.

	2.	The abolition movement was substantially driven by enslaved and formerly enslaved people themselves. Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian Revolution (1791), Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, David Walker’s Appeal, and hundreds of documented slave rebellions that made the system economically and socially untenable. Walsh erases their agency entirely while condemning the erasure of African agency in the trade itself. He can’t have it both ways.

The Real Agenda

Walsh states plainly that the left uses slavery to give themselves “moral justification to do whatever they want” to white people, and that this documentary is his answer to that. He told you the conclusion before he showed you the evidence. That’s not history. That’s a legal brief. Every fact he selected, every fact he omitted, every piece of footage he chose was in service of a predetermined verdict: White Americans owe nothing. The debt is cancelled.

That may feel satisfying. But a historian’s job is to follow the evidence to the conclusion, not select evidence to reach a conclusion already decided.

What a Complete History Actually Shows

Slavery is ancient and universal. Walsh is right. African kingdoms participated actively in the Transatlantic trade. Walsh is right. But the specific institution of chattel slavery in the American South, race-based, hereditary, legally codified, and designed for perpetual reproduction, was historically unique in its design and its multigenerational demographic consequences. Walsh is silent on this. The wealth gap, incarceration disparities, redlining, and systemic disadvantages Black Americans face today are documented downstream effects of that specific institution, not vague grievance politics. Walsh dismisses this entirely.

You don’t have to accept guilt for history you didn’t create. But understanding what actually happened, all of it, is not a political act. It’s just intellectual honesty. Walsh is giving you half the map and telling you it’s the whole territory.

Read The Half Has Never Been Told by Edward Baptist. Read The Slave Trade by Hugh Thomas, a conservative historian. Then come back and watch this documentary again. You’ll see the architecture of the argument much more clearly.


The truth doesn’t need a political home. Demand all of it.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

The Horrible Fate of John Casor, The First Black Man to be Declared Slave for Life in America
Black people in early America weren’t slaves. After this lawsuit, they could be

Kat Eschner
March 8, 2017

No images of Casor survive to the present day. Tobacco fields like this one, however, would have been what he saw daily. 

The only date definitely connected to John Casor’s life is this day in 1654 or 1655. It’s not when he was born, when he achieved something or when he died. It’s when he became a slave.

Casor was originally an indentured servant, which meant he was practically a slave in some senses. But what was bought or sold wasn’t him, it was his contract of indenture, which obligated him to work for its holder for the period it set. At the end of that time, indentured servants—who could be of any race—were considered legally free and sent out into the world.

This might sound like a rough deal, but indenture was how the British colonizers who lived in what would later become the United States managed to populate the land and get enough people to do the back-breaking work of farming crops like tobacco in the South.

People who survived their period of indenture (many didn’t) went on to live free lives in the colonies, often after receiving some kind of small compensation like clothes, land or tools to help set them up, writes Ariana Kyl for Today I Found Out.

That was the incentive that caused many poor whites to indenture themselves and their families and move to the so-called New World. But Africans who were indentured were often captured and brought over against their will. That's what happened to the holder of Casor’s indenture, Anthony Johnson. Johnson served out his contract and went on to run his own tobacco farm and hold his own indentured servants, among them Casor. At this time, the colony of Virginia had very few black people in it: Johnson was one of the original 20.

After a disagreement about whether or not Casor's contract was lapsed, a court ruled in favor of Johnson and Casor saw the status of his indenture turn into slavery, where he—not his contract—was considered property. Casor claimed that he had served his indenture of “seaven or Eight years” and seven more years on top of that. The court sided with Johnson, who claimed that Casor was his slave for life.

So Casor became the first person to be arbitrarily declared a slave for life in the U.S. (An earlier case had ended with a man named John Punch being declared a slave for life as a punishment for trying to escape his indentured servitude. His fellow escapees, who were white, were not punished in this way.) Of course, as Wesleyan University notes, “the Transatlantic slave trade from Africa to the Americas had been around for over a century already, originating around 1500.” Slaves, usually captured and sold by other African tribes, were transported across the Atlantic to the Americas, the university’s blog notes. Around 11 million people were transported from 1500 to 1850, mostly to Brazil and the Caribbean islands. If they arrived in America, originally they became indentured servants; if they arrived elsewhere, they became slaves.

Casor’s story is particularly grim in hindsight. His slip into slavery would be followed by many, many other people of African descent who were declared property in what became the United States. It was a watershed moment in the history of institutional slavery.

“About seven years later, Virginia made this practice legal for everyone, in 1661, by making it state law for any free white, black or Indian to be able to own slaves, along with indentured servants,” Kyl writes. The step from there to a racialized idea of slavery wasn’t a huge one, she writes, and by the time Johnson died in 1670, his race was used to justify giving his plantation to a white man rather than Johnson’s children by his wife, Mary. He was “not a citizen of the colony,” a judge ruled, because he was black.
